stances.claim: Under the Medellin v. Texas doctrine, the VFA is not enforceable in the US because the US Congress has enacted no implementing law, the VFA is not self-executory by its terms, and it was never even ratified by the US Senate.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal-application: imports a US Supreme Court holding into PH legal analysis to argue reciprocal non-enforceability
stances.evidence: Medellin v. Texas (March 25, 2008), CJ Roberts opinion; verified non-ratification by US Senate; absence of US implementing legislation

stances.claim: The MDT, though ratified by the US Senate, is likewise unenforceable in the US because it is not self-executory by its terms and has no US implementing law.
stances.rhetorical_move: parallel-application of the same Medellin test
stances.evidence: Treaty text analysis under Medellin's two-prong standard

stances.claim: Because Sec. 25, Art. XVIII of the 1987 Constitution requires the other contracting state to recognize the agreement as a treaty, and because the US no longer enforces the VFA as one, the Philippines as a self-respecting sovereign has no choice but to deem the VFA and MDT unenforceable here.
stances.rhetorical_move: constitutional-reciprocity argument grounded in sovereign dignity
stances.evidence: Sec. 25, Art. XVIII; Medellin doctrine read as supervening to Bayan v. Zamora

stances.claim: Justice Scalia's confession that he believed the US Supreme Court is tasked to enforce only US Constitution and US laws — not cross-border concepts without implementing statutes — exemplifies the philosophical foundation of the Medellin doctrine.
stances.rhetorical_move: anecdotal authority: uses a personal encounter to humanize a doctrinal point
stances.evidence: May 17, 2006 personal conversation in Washington DC

notable_anecdotes: The author's May 17, 2006 Washington DC visit to US Justice Antonin Scalia, where Scalia declined the invitation to the Global Forum on Liberty and Prosperity by explaining 'I am useless in international meetings because I believe that our Supreme Court is tasked to enforce only the US Constitution and US laws, not cross-border concepts that do not find implementing US statutes' — used as personal-encounter evidence of the philosophical undercurrent of Medellin.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban responds to President Duterte's surprise six-month suspension of the VFA abrogation (Diplomatic Note No. 2020-2622, June 1, 2020) by tracing the layered history of the VFA (Senate-concurred May 27, 1999; upheld in Bayan v. Zamora, Oct 10, 2000, from which he recused due to ties to petitioner Salonga) and the MDT (Aug 30, 1951), then walks through the 2006 Daniel Smith rape case and the Romulo-Kenney transfer of Smith to the US Embassy -- which was invalidated in Nicolas v. Romulo (Feb 11, 2009) yet strangely left Smith in embassy custody pending diplomatic agreement. He pivots to the dispositive supervening doctrine: Medellin v. Texas (March 25, 2008, CJ Roberts) held that a treaty, even one ratified by the US Senate, is not enforceable as US domestic federal law unless Congress enacts implementing legislation or the treaty is by its terms self-executory and Senate-ratified as such. Applying this test, he argues the VFA fails on all counts (no US Senate ratification, no implementing law, not self-executory) and the MDT also fails (no implementing law, not self-executory), making both treaties unenforceable in the US. Because Sec. 25, Art. XVIII of the 1987 Constitution requires the other contracting state to 'recognize as a treaty' any agreement permitting foreign troops, the Philippines as a self-respecting sovereign has no choice but to deem both treaties unenforceable here. He punctuates the argument with a personal anecdote about Justice Antonin Scalia's May 17, 2006 confession in Washington that he was 'useless in international meetings' because the US Supreme Court enforces only the US Constitution and US statutes -- and closes by wondering whether this Medellin conundrum is what truly informed Duterte's Feb 11 abrogation.
